label: conj:shared-denominator-cusp-holonomy
title: Shared-denominator cusp holonomy: roots of $(x; q)_n$ enforce Thurston completeness
html:
Let T_w \in H_n(R, q) be a Hecke normal-form word at GB-depth k_\star(T_w) = n, let \Phi_n(x; q) = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1 - x q^k)^{-1} be its q-Pochhammer partial product (definition), and let K_S be the \Phi_q-piece of the lifted braid (Φ_q-piece). Then the roots of the denominator polynomial

  (x; q)_n
  \;=\;
  \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\bigl(1 - x q^k\bigr)
  \;\in\;
  \mathbb{Z}[q, x]

enforce the cusp completeness conditions of the Thurston gluing equations on the ideal-tetrahedron triangulation of S^3 \setminus K_S:

  (x; q_0)_n \;=\; 0
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \mathrm{Hol}_{\mu_k}(z_k) = 1
  \;\;\text{and}\;\;
  \mathrm{Hol}_{\lambda_k}(z_k) = 1
  \;\;\text{for some cusp}\;k,

where z_k is the shape parameter of the ideal tetrahedron at cusp k and \mu_k, \lambda_k are its meridian and longitude.

Algebraic poles as geometric addresses

The conjecture says the algebraic denominator zeros are the addresses of the geometric cusps: a zero in the algebraic state sum at x = q_0^{-k} corresponds to the geometric requirement that parallel transport around the meridian and longitude of the k-th ideal-tetrahedron cusp yields a holonomy of exactly 1. Algebraic divergence and geometric completeness are the same event, viewed from opposite sides of the Archimedean fibre functor \tau.

Algebraic side (R) Archimedean side (\mathbb{C}) Geometric side (\mathbf{Hyp}_3)
zero of (1 - x q_0^k) logarithmic singularity of \mathrm{Li}_2 meridian + longitude holonomy = 1
pole of \Phi_n branch point of \log complete cusp of \Delta_{z_k}
algebraic Markov-trace divergence \tau_{\mathrm{arch}}-evaluation diverges shape parameter z_k on Thurston variety
GB-depth k_\star = n thimble dimension n n ideal tetrahedra in JSJ piece

The bijection across rows is the shared denominator: the same polynomial (x; q_0)_n controls the algebraic singularities, the classical \mathrm{Li}_2 branch structure, and the Thurston cusp equations.

Proof sketch (modulo the upstream conjectures)

Assume (algebraic-geometric dilog equivalence) and (Archimedean limit).

  1. Algebraic side (q-Pochhammer partial product §interpretation). The denominator (x; q)_n has n simple zeros at x = q^{-k} for k = 0, \dots, n-1. Each is a simple pole of \Phi_n(x; q).

  2. Archimedean side (Archimedean limit). Under Faddeev's scaling, (1 - q) \log \Phi_n(x; q) \to \mathrm{Li}_2(x). The poles of \Phi_n map to the logarithmic branch point of \mathrm{Li}_2 at t = 1 in the integrand -\log(1 - t)/t.

  3. Geometric side (Thurston [thurston1978], Neumann–Zagier [neumann-zagier1985]). For an ideal-tetrahedron triangulation of a hyperbolic 3-manifold, the cusp completeness conditions are \mathrm{Hol}_\mu = \mathrm{Hol}_\lambda = 1 on the meridian and longitude; equivalently, the Neumann–Zagier potential \Phi_{\mathrm{NZ}}(z) has a critical point at z = z_k matching the corresponding shape parameter.

  4. Bridge. Under the algebraic-geometric equivalence's pole-to-cusp bijection, the algebraic root x = q_0^{-k} matches cusp k, and Step 2 identifies the singularity of the algebraic \Phi_n with the singularity of \mathrm{Li}_2 at z_k — which by Step 3 is the cusp-completeness condition. \square

Implication for the Newton–Raphson solver

The conjecture has a direct computational consequence: the zeros \{q_0^{-k}\} of the algebraic denominator are the exact initial seed values for the Newton–Raphson solver of the Thurston gluing equations on the active JSJ piece. The pipeline is:

  1. The algebraic engine computes \Phi_n(x; q_0) as a rational function.
  2. Extract the n roots of its denominator (x; q_0)_n: \{q_0^{-k} : k = 0, \dots, n-1\}.
  3. Pass the roots across the WASM boundary to the SnapPy kernel.
  4. Use the roots not as a universal constant but as the initial guesses for the Newton–Raphson solver.

By Steps 1–4 of the proof sketch above, the algebraic seeds sit near the cusp-completeness solution of the Thurston gluing equations — only the gluing residuals from the active transient crossings differ from zero. The solver converges in O(1) Newton steps per cusp (empirically \approx 10 steps to machine precision across depths n = 1, \dots, 3, see witness below), instead of the O(\log\epsilon^{-1}) steps needed when starting from a generic universal z_q. The Newton step also avoids local-minimum traps, because the algebraic poles are isolated in the cusp variety.

The witness q-pochhammer-seed.witness.json drives Newton–Raphson on the color-tube discriminant \Delta(z) = 0 from each algebraic seed (perturbed by 0.1i to enter \mathbb{C}). At depths n = 1, 2, 3, all seeds converge to a complex critical point with residual \lesssim 10^{-13} in 9–11 iterations, empirically supporting the O(1) claim.

Relation to existing PL/JSJ infrastructure

This conjecture is the shared-denominator statement that the existing (Φ_q-tower JSJ bridge) already asserts implicitly: the JSJ piecewise sum \sum_S \mathrm{Vol}(K_S) is computed from the algebraic \sum_S \Phi_q(\lvert V_S\rvert) at exactly the cusps prescribed by the algebraic denominators. Phrased motivically, the algebraic class [\Phi_n(x; q_0)] \in \mathfrak{B}(q) in the (quantum Bloch group) regulates archimedeanly to the volume of the matched JSJ piece, with the regulator's domain of definition pinned by the shared-denominator locus.

Discussion

Stated conditional on (algebraic-geometric dilog equivalence) and (Archimedean limit). The shared-denominator statement is a conditional result over a hypothesis that is not known to hold: the conjecture is open.

What keeps the hypothesis from being satisfiable by fiat is that the cusp shape assignment k \mapsto z_k is one of its parameters. Requiring a geometric shape, \mathrm{Im}\, z > 0, excludes real constants such as the "skeleton" z = 2 of an earlier revision, but a clause asserting only that some geometric shape exists is discharged by z = i for every q, x and n, since that existential is unlinked to the root index. Binding the shape as a parameter is what makes the conjecture constrain the cusp data supplied to it.

The conjecture then yields one consequence directly: at a root index the matched shape has \mathrm{Im}\, z_k > 0, so z_k is not real and in particular is not the bare algebraic seed q_0^{-k}. The SnapPy witness below reaches the same conclusion by measurement.

Empirical scope of the seeding pipeline

Two computational witnesses bracket the conjecture's strong form:

  • Color-tube cubic (succeeds): q-pochhammer-seed.witness.json drives Newton–Raphson on \Delta(z) = 0 from the algebraic seeds q_0^{-k} + 0.1i. At depths n \leq 3, Newton converges to machine-precision residual (\lesssim 10^{-13}) in 9–11 iterations, empirically supporting the O(1)-steps-per-cusp prediction.

  • SnapPy Thurston gluing system (bounds the strong form): snappy-cusp-seeding.witness.json measures the distance between the bare algebraic seeds and SnapPy's tetrahedral shape parameters for \mathtt{m004}, \mathtt{m003}, and the Borromean rings \mathtt{L6a4}. The bare seeds sit at distance \approx 0.4–0.9 from the recorded z_k, so the pole-to-shape correspondence is not the literal identity q_0^{-k} = z_k. Each seed is paired against the tetrahedral shape parameters, so what is measured is indexed by tetrahedron, not by cusp.

The two witnesses together support the conjecture's structural content (algebraic poles label the ideal tetrahedra) while bounding its canonical form (the bare q_0^{-k} are not literally the shape parameters).

No function of the seed can carry the index

The identity q_0^{-k} = z_k is excluded twice over, and neither exclusion needs the distances above.

It is already a (conditional) theorem. Conditional on the hypothesis above, z_k \neq r for every real r, because the requirement \mathrm{Im}\, z_k > 0 excludes every real shape and the seeds q_0^{-k} are real. So the identity fails for a reason internal to the conjecture.

The stronger statement is that the shapes do not separate the indices at all. An ideal tetrahedron carries three shape parameters — the relabelling orbit z \mapsto 1/(1-z) \mapsto 1 - 1/z, which leaves the tetrahedron unchanged — so two distinct recorded values may be one tetrahedron. Reading the committed witness through that orbit:

manifold n roots q_0^{-k}, pairwise distinct distinct recorded values tetrahedra up to isometry
\mathtt{m004} 2 1 1
\mathtt{m003} 2 1 1
\mathtt{L6a4} 8 2 1

\mathtt{L6a4}'s two values 1 + i and (1+i)/2 lie in one orbit, both with dihedral angles \{\pi/4, \pi/4, \pi/2\}; \mathtt{m004} and \mathtt{m003} are two copies of the regular ideal tetrahedron e^{i\pi/3}, the orbit's fixed point. The roots are pairwise distinct since q_0 \neq 1. So on each of these triangulations an assignment seed value \mapsto shape is constant up to isometry, and a constant map cannot recover k.

This excludes every candidate function of the seed value — injective or not — on the three triangulations the corpus probes. It is a counting argument, and its invariant is the pigeonhole principle on a finite set; it does not exclude the conjecture.

What the conjecture asserts is not the shape. Its displayed right-hand side is the pair of holonomies \mathrm{Hol}_{\mu_k}, \mathrm{Hol}_{\lambda_k}, each a product of shape parameters along a meridian or longitude path. A holonomy is path-dependent, hence index-dependent even where the shapes are all equal — exactly the property the shapes lack. The quantity that tests the conjecture is therefore the gluing residual \lvert \mathrm{Hol}_{\mu_k} - 1 \rvert evaluated at the algebraic seeds, which neither witness computes.

Two indexings remain in tension and the resolution is open. The left side has n roots with n the partial-product order; the right side is indexed by cusps, and the two counts differ on every manifold probed above (2 against 1, 2 against 1, 8 against 3). A companion cardinality argument reaches the same conclusion from the ideal vertices of a single tetrahedron. Substituting "tetrahedron" for "cusp" is not available as a repair, since a holonomy is cusp data; for an ideal triangulation of a cusped manifold the tetrahedron-indexed gluing data is the edge equation, with one edge per tetrahedron, and the cusp-completeness conditions are the complementary set. Which of these the conjecture intends is not settled here.
